title: Ideas Are Plants and Buildings
tagline: growth, foundations and collapse in plans and organisations
why: When English speakers talk about plans, careers, arguments and institutions, they rarely use neutral words: ideas take root, companies grow, theories have foundations and arguments collapse. These images carry judgement, so choosing the right one sharpens your persuasion.
know: eight key idioms of growth and construction, such as bear fruit, lay the foundations and a house of cards
everyday hidden metaphors such as a growing company, a solid case and the framework of a theory
understand: that plant images stress time, nurture and natural development, while building images stress structure and strength
that the same idea can be praised or attacked by choosing a different image
able: describe how a plan, career or organisation develops, succeeds or fails
use these idioms with the right verbs and in the right register
discuss songs, poems and stories that use gardens, walls and cracks
mistakes: We must cut the problem in the bud.
We must nip the problem in the bud. The verb is fixed; a bud is a young flower.
The project finally bore fruit. English uses bear, not give.
She lives in a tower of ivory.
She lives in an ivory tower. Fixed word order, and it's a criticism, not a compliment.
The company built the bases for future growth.
The company laid the foundations for future growth. Lay + foundations is the natural collocation.
Our plan is a castle of cards.
Our plan is a house of cards. Castle is a literal translation from French or Spanish.
bigidea: Ideas and organisations are often plants. They start as seeds, take root, grow, branch out, flourish, bear fruit or wither. This image emphasises time, care and natural development.
They are also buildings. They have foundations, frameworks, pillars and cracks, and they can be constructed, supported or collapse. This image emphasises structure, solidity and design.

Choosing between them is a rhetorical decision. A politician who says a policy will grow sounds patient; one who says it rests on solid foundations sounds careful. Critics attack the same idea by saying its foundations are shaky or that it withered on the vine.
hidden: We're a growing company with offices in three provinces.
She has had a flourishing career in architecture.
It takes time to construct a convincing argument.
Darwin provided the framework for modern biology.
Once the key witness changed her story, the whole theory collapsed.
The project withered when the funding dried up.

expressions.meaning: create the basic conditions that later success depends on
expressions.example: Those early years in a small law firm laid the foundations for her career as a judge.
expressions.bend: Flexible: laid solid foundations, the foundations were laid, lay the groundwork. Lay is the natural verb.
expressions.note: Lay the groundwork is very close; foundations sounds more permanent and important.

expressions.example: The idea of a four-day week has begun to take root in some Canadian firms.
expressions.bend: Tense is flexible: took root, has taken root. No article and no plural: not take a root or take roots.
expressions.note: Can be negative: prejudice took root. Compare put down roots, which means settle in a place.

expressions.meaning: produce good results, usually after time and effort
expressions.example: Years of quiet diplomacy finally bore fruit with a ceasefire.
expressions.bend: The verb inflects: bore fruit, has borne fruit. Fruit stays singular.
expressions.note: Formal. In casual speech people say pay off. Related: the fruits of your labour, the rewards of hard work.

expressions.meaning: stop a problem at an early stage before it grows
expressions.example: When the first complaints about bullying came in, the principal nipped it in the bud.
expressions.bend: The object varies: nip the rumour in the bud. Nip and bud are fixed.
expressions.note: Often garbled as nip it in the butt, a well-known mistake. The image is a gardener pinching off a bud before it flowers.

expressions.e: the cracks are starting to show
expressions.meaning: problems in something that looked strong are becoming visible
expressions.example: Six months after the merger, the cracks are starting to show in the leadership team.
expressions.bend: Very flexible: cracks appeared, cracks in the coalition, paper over the cracks.
expressions.note: Paper over the cracks means hide problems without fixing them, a favourite image in political journalism.

expressions.meaning: a plan or organisation so weak it could collapse at any moment
expressions.example: The investigation revealed that the fund was a house of cards built on borrowed money.
expressions.bend: Bends well: collapse like a house of cards, the whole house of cards came down.
expressions.note: Strongly critical. Also the title of a British political novel and TV series about scheming politicians, later remade in the US.

expressions.meaning: a privileged place cut off from practical everyday life, especially academia
expressions.example: Critics say the report was written in an ivory tower by people who have never run a small business.
expressions.bend: Often used as an adjective: ivory-tower academics, ivory-tower thinking.
expressions.note: Usually a criticism of academics or experts. Saying I work in an ivory tower about yourself is self-mocking.

expressions.meaning: create better relations between groups who disagree or distrust each other
expressions.example: The new mayor has worked hard to build bridges between city hall and Indigenous communities.
expressions.bend: Flexible: bridge-building, build bridges with someone. The opposite is burn your bridges.
expressions.note: Positive and common in politics and diplomacy. Don't confuse it with cross that bridge when we come to it, which is about dealing with problems later.

culture.how: The Montreal-born songwriter treats imperfection as a crack in a structure, but the crack is not a failure: it is what allows light to enter. The song flips the usual negative meaning of cracks into a message of hope.
culture.ask: Can a flaw or failure ever be a strength? Give an example from work, sport or family life.

culture.how: The Canadian songwriter wrote it after seeing a beautiful view in Hawaii spoiled by a car park. Here building is the villain: paving and construction destroy the natural paradise that growth metaphors usually celebrate.
culture.ask: Is building always progress? Think of a place near you that changed. Was something lost?

culture.how: After a novel full of wars, disasters and foolish optimism, the hero concludes that the best response is simply to tend our own garden. The garden becomes a metaphor for modest, practical work instead of grand theories.
culture.ask: Do you agree that modest, practical work is wiser than big theories about the world? Why or why not?

culture.how: Two New England neighbours meet each spring to repair the stone wall between their farms. The speaker questions why the wall is needed at all, while his neighbour repeats an old saying about fences. The wall becomes a metaphor for the barriers people build between themselves.
culture.ask: Do good boundaries make good neighbours, colleagues or families? Where do you build walls, and where bridges?

culture.how: A farmer scatters seed: some lands on a path, some on rocky ground, some among thorns and some on good soil, where it grows well. Jesus uses it to show how a message takes root in some listeners and not others, an early model of ideas as seeds.
culture.ask: Why do some ideas take root in a team or community while others never grow? What makes good soil?

match.r: create the basis for later success
match.why: Foundations come first and support everything built on top.
A plant that takes root is stable and will keep growing.
Fruit is the reward that comes after a long period of growth.
Pinch off the bud and the flower never opens.

match.l: the cracks are starting to show
match.why: Cracks are the first sign that a structure is weakening.
One touch and a tower of playing cards falls down.

match.r: a place cut off from real life
match.why: Ivory is precious and the tower is high above ordinary people.
A bridge connects two sides that were separated.

sort.h: Sort each expression by the image underneath it: is it a plant or a building?

items.why: A tree grows new branches in new directions.
A seed is the start of a plant.
The roots of the grass: the base of a plant community.
A bud is a young flower.
Foundations are the base of a building.
A pillar holds up a building.
A fragile structure, built of playing cards.

items.w: the cracks are starting to show

pick.q: After ten years as an accountant, Priya wanted to ___ into wedding photography.
pick.why: Branch out into: expand into a new area of activity.

pick.q: The lawyer's careless remark planted ___ in the jury's mind.
pick.why: A seed of doubt: a small uncertainty that may grow.

pick.q: The movement began with ___ volunteers knocking on doors, not with big donors.
pick.why: Grassroots: ordinary people at the base of a movement.

pick.q: Grandpa coached minor hockey for forty years and was ___ in our small town.
pick.why: A pillar of the community: a respected person others rely on.

pick.q: If students start skipping class, deal with it now and ___.
pick.why: Nip it in the bud: stop it before it grows.

pick.q: The economists' proposals sound elegant, but they come from ___ and ignore how families actually budget.
pick.why: An ivory tower: a place cut off from practical life.

pick.q: Once one big client left, the company's finances collapsed like ___.
pick.why: Collapse like a house of cards: fall apart suddenly because it was fragile.

pick.q: Retirement is the time to enjoy ___ after decades of hard work.
pick.why: The fruits of your labour: the rewards of your work.

spot.q: We need to nip this rumour in the butt before the press hears about it.
spot.why: Nip it in the bud: a bud is a young flower. In the butt is a famous garble.

spot.q: Her research finally bore fruits after a decade in the lab.
spot.why: Bear fruit is fixed with singular fruit.

spot.q: The new recycling habit took roots quickly in our neighbourhood.
spot.why: Take root: no article, no plural.

spot.q: After the bitter election, the two parties are trying to construct bridges.
spot.why: The idiom is build bridges. Construct sounds like real engineering.

spot.q: The minister's plan is a tower of cards that will fall at the first recession.
spot.why: In English it's always a house of cards.

type.q: The civil rights campaigns of the 1960s laid the ___ for later equality laws.
type.why: Lay the foundations (or groundwork): create the base for later progress.

type.q: The tradition took ___ in Nova Scotia and spread west from there.
type.why: Take root (or take hold): become established.

type.q: Professors in their ivory ___ rarely see how students actually live.
type.why: An ivory tower: a place cut off from everyday reality.

type.q: Their marriage looked perfect, but the ___ were starting to show by the second year.
type.why: The cracks are starting to show: hidden problems appear.

type.q: The negotiators spent months trying to build ___ between the union and management.
type.why: Build bridges: improve relations between two sides.

type.q: The scheme was a house of ___ and collapsed as soon as interest rates rose.
type.why: A house of cards: a fragile structure ready to fall.

opts: The government is accused of papering over the cracks.
The government is accused of painting over the fissures.
The government is accused of papering under the cracks.
bend.why: Paper over the cracks is a natural extension of the cracks image: hide problems without fixing them.

opts: Their partnership has well and truly borne fruits.
Their partnership has well and truly borne fruit.
Their partnership has well and truly carried fruit.
bend.why: Adding well and truly is fine, but the core bear fruit stays: borne fruit, singular.

opts: Critics dismissed it as ivory-castle thinking.
Critics dismissed it as tower-of-ivory thinking.
Critics dismissed it as ivory-tower thinking.
bend.why: Ivory tower works naturally as a hyphenated adjective: ivory-tower thinking.

opts: The campaign enjoys strong grassroots support.
The campaign enjoys strong roots-of-grass support.
The campaign enjoys strong grassroots supports.
bend.why: Grassroots is used as an adjective before uncountable support.

talk: Think of a project in your life that took years to bear fruit. What laid the foundations for it?
Voltaire's hero decides to tend his own garden. Is modest, practical work better than grand theories? Discuss with an example.
Leonard Cohen suggests that cracks can be good because they let light in. Do you agree? When did a crack in your plans lead somewhere better?
Role-play: you are a new manager, and two departments don't trust each other. Explain to Bill how you will build bridges.
Are universities ivory towers? Argue one side, then the other.

match.why: The roots of the grass are at ground level, like ordinary members.
Pillars hold a building up, as such people support a community.
A tree grows new branches in new directions.

match.r: a small first feeling of uncertainty
match.why: A seed is tiny but can grow into something big.
Fruit is what you harvest after work and patience.
Solid structures are hard to knock down, like good arguments.

pick.q: The bakery did so well that the owners decided to ___ into catering.
pick.why: Branch out into: expand into a new line of business.

pick.q: Mrs. Okafor has run the food bank for decades; she's truly ___.
pick.why: A pillar of the community: a respected person others depend on.

pick.q: The petition was a ___ effort organised by parents, not politicians.
One small inconsistency in his story planted ___ in my mind.
pick.why: Plant a seed of doubt: start a feeling of uncertainty.

pick.q: With the DNA evidence, the Crown now has ___ against the accused.
pick.why: A solid case: a strong argument supported by evidence.

pick.q: After forty years on the farm, they finally sat back to enjoy ___.
pick.why: The fruits of their labour: the rewards of long work.

spot.q: The retired doctor is a pillow of the community in our town.
spot.why: A pillar supports a building. A pillow is for sleeping!

spot.q: Our firm is branching off into renewable energy next year.
spot.why: Branch out into: expand. Branch off means a road or path splits away.

spot.q: His testimony planted a grain of doubt in the jury's mind.
spot.why: The usual phrase is a seed of doubt; you plant seeds. Compare a grain of truth.

spot.q: After years of patient research, the vaccine project finally gave fruit.
spot.why: English uses bear: bore fruit. Gave fruit is a literal translation.

type.q: The rumours planted a ___ of doubt about the coach's future.
type.why: A seed of doubt: a small uncertainty that can grow.

type.q: Dr. Ahmed was a ___ of the community, delivering half the babies in town.
type.why: A pillar of the community: someone others rely on.

type.q: Once you've paid off the mortgage, you can enjoy the ___ of your labour.
type.why: The fruits of your labour: the rewards of hard work.

type.q: Her lawyers built a ___ case, backed by emails and witness statements.
type.why: A solid (or watertight) case is strong and well supported.

type.q: The opposition's argument ___ completely when the real figures were published.
type.why: Arguments are buildings: they collapse or crumble.

type.q: It's best to ___ bad habits in the bud.
type.why: Nip something in the bud: stop it early.

bank.q: The city's composting program has finally ___ in the suburbs.
bank.why: Take root: become established and accepted.

bank.q: Without a real business plan, the start-up was ___ waiting to fall.
bank.why: A house of cards: something fragile that could collapse.

bank.q: The peace talks finally ___ after years of patient negotiation.
bank.why: Bear fruit: produce good results after long effort.

bank.q: A good principal can ___ between angry parents and teachers.
bank.why: Build bridges: improve relations between two sides.

bank.q: Commentators who live in ___ rarely understand the cost of groceries.
bank.why: An ivory tower: a privileged place cut off from ordinary life.

bank.q: Our early savings habits ___ for a comfortable retirement.
bank.why: Lay the foundations for: create the base for later success.

bank.q: The coach noticed the locker-room tension and ___ before the playoffs.
bank.why: Nip it in the bud: deal with a problem early.

bank.q: By the third year, ___ in their business partnership, and they argued constantly.
opts: the cracks were starting to show
bank.a: the cracks were starting to show
bank.why: The cracks are starting to show: problems become visible.

bank.q: His decision to ___ out into politics surprised everyone at the law firm.
bank.why: Branch out: move into a new area.

bank.q: These reforms will lay the ___ for a fairer tax system.
bank.why: Lay the foundations: create the base for something.

bank.q: That one late payment sowed a ___ of doubt about the supplier.
bank.why: Sow or plant a seed of doubt: start a feeling of uncertainty.

bank.q: Political change often starts at the ___ level, in kitchens and church halls.
bank.why: Grassroots: among ordinary people rather than leaders.

bank.q: Once the main witness withdrew, the case ___ like a house of cards.
bank.why: Collapse like a house of cards: fall apart suddenly.

bank.q: The board hopes the new strategy will bare fruit by next spring.
bank.why: Bear (produce) fruit, not bare (uncovered). Will + base form: will bear fruit.

bank.q: The new hiring policy has started to take root across all our branches.
bank.why: Correct: take root means become established.

bank.q: Academics in their ivory castles often ignore practical problems.
bank.why: The fixed phrase is an ivory tower.

bank.q: We managed to nip the complaint in the bloom before it reached head office.
bank.why: Nip it in the bud: stop it before the flower opens.

bank.a: Years of hard work finally bore fruit for the team.
bank.why: Subject + finally + bore fruit + for someone.

bank.a: She laid the foundations for a successful business.
bank.why: Lay the foundations for + noun phrase.

bank.a: The rumour planted a seed of doubt in my mind.
bank.why: Plant a seed of doubt in someone's mind.
